D1: Limited review of an authored synthetic packet: both saves achieve their separate goals and persist after refresh for the owner. Consider 'Save checklist' and 'Save project answers' so scope stays available at the action without merging distinct permissions or operations. D3: Limited review of an authored synthetic packet: deletion completes with the named workspace removed and the other retained. The dialog explains irreversibility, requires the correct name, and supports cancellation without data changes. The packet supports the cancellation and target-isolation portions but does not report an incorrect-name test. Keyboard and assistive-technology operation remain untested. D5: Limited review of an authored synthetic packet: comparison requires applying presets before size/format details appear, and two traces show loss of the unsaved title with neither switching back nor Undo restoring it. This is a high-severity usability concern with high confidence in the supplied behavior: comparison interrupts draft continuity, although intended title semantics are unknown. Saving a copy first is a working workaround, not evidence of frictionless completion. Recommend exposing details before Apply and preserving the draft title during comparison; if renaming is intentional, make it a separate explicit choice with recovery. Preserve preset setting application and saved-copy behavior. Proposed acceptance: begin with an unsaved custom title, inspect both presets, return to editing, and verify the title and draft remain intact; deliberately apply settings and verify only disclosed changes. If inspection still mutates the draft or title recovery fails, the remedy fails. Export execution and human effects remain untested.
D6: Limited review of an authored synthetic packet: 192 frames correctly yields eight seconds at 24 fps and 6.4 seconds at 30 fps. Exact-frame control works. A medium-severity usability concern, with high confidence in the supplied information gap, is that seconds and frame-rate consequences are absent at the duration decision; human errors are unmeasured. Recommend a derived seconds value and a clear statement of what a frame-rate change preserves, retaining integer frame entry. Do not automatically preserve seconds: the professional requirement leaves that policy unspecified, and doing so could change intentional frame counts. Proposed acceptance: 192 frames displays 8 seconds at 24 fps and, under the current fixed-frame policy, 6.4 seconds at 30 fps; the count remains 192 and the policy is visible. Incorrect or stale derived values would refute the remedy. A neutral task involving a frame-rate change could test comprehension; no human performance claim is supported.
